description: A security engineering manager must finalize the production rollout policy for workload-identity enforcement across internal Kubernetes services after a successful pilot, with input from application engineering and compliance operations.

shared_context.S1: The workload-identity pilot completed successfully in the staging cluster.
shared_context.S2: Riley owns the production policy decision for workload-identity enforcement.
shared_context.S3: The production rollout plan must specify enforcement behavior, service handling, emergency access, and audit settings.
shared_context.S4: As part of the standard security sign-off, Riley reviews the plan with application platform engineering and compliance operations before publishing it.

PF1.text: While debugging an unrelated deployment this morning, Casey confirmed that the batch-ledger service still reads a static Kubernetes secret and will fail under enforcement; the migration is ready only if batch-ledger is excluded for exactly 14 days, and Casey has not filed the compatibility note yet.

PF2.text: Morgan confirmed with the audit team today that production enforcement must retain denied-token events for exactly 180 days, enable denied-token logging, and require two-person approval for every break-glass access; these requirements are not yet recorded in the rollout plan.

acceptance_conditions: Workload-identity enforcement must be enabled in production.
The rollout must use enforcement with the batch-ledger exception.
The batch-ledger exception must expire after exactly 14 days.
Audit evidence must be retained for exactly 180 days.
Break-glass access must require two-person approval.
A batch-ledger compatibility commitment must be recorded.
The audit requirements must be represented in the rollout plan.
The batch-ledger compatibility fact must be cited in the decision justification.

content_checks.C8: any(c['type'] in ['compatibility_note', 'documentation'] or ('compatibility note' in c['detail'] and 'batch-ledger' in c['detail']) for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: The successful pilot gives no reason to name an exception, while PF1 changes the service list to exactly batch-ledger, the exception duration to exactly 14 days, and the plan to include a compatibility commitment.

The shared rollout plan does not specify audit controls, while PF2 changes logging to enabled, retention to exactly 180 days, break-glass access to two-person approval, and the plan to include those audit requirements.
